records.abstract: This thesis investigates the prevalence and predictors that contribute to elevated burnout scores.Hence it contributes to Good Health and Well-being -third goal of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.By applying Copenhagen Burnout Inventory and adapting Job Demands-Resources model, the thesis shows that the burnout in the Information Technology sector can be explained through organizational, psychological and technological demands and resources.By integrating qualitative interview findings, regression and predictive analysis, the thesis brings a comprehensive framework for understanding the presence of burnout in IT as well as the key drivers that contribute to its elevation.This way companies can use those for making the work environments healthier and productive which aligns with the eighth Sustainable Development Goal (Decent Work and Economic Growth).Machine Learning models, including Linear Regression, Extreme Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, Support Vector Regression and Neural Networks were developed to predict burnout levels, which aligns with ninth goal of Sustainable Development Goals (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure).Even though the used models didn't perform so well, the thesis suggests that Linear Regression provides considerable accuracy, therefore, it can be utilized for predicting burnout in IT employees and achieving acceptable results.

records.title: Smart Employee Monitoring System: Machine Learning-Driven Workforce Analytics and Risk Prediction
records.abstract: Employee attrition, burnout, and low engagement can affect workforce stability and organizational performance. This paper presents a Smart Employee Monitoring System (SEMS) that combines machine learning, explainable AI, and natural language processing to support employee-related analysis. The system evaluates employee information to predict attrition risk and identify possible burnout conditions using multiple factors such as work patterns, job satisfaction, and stress indicators. Six machine learning algorithms Decision Tree, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Naive Bayes, and KNearest Neighbors are used for attrition prediction, with Random Forest achieving approximately 92% accuracy in the project evaluation. The system also uses SHAP-based explanations to show the factors influencing predictions and TextBlob-based sentiment analysis to analyze employee feedback. A role-based architecture provides separate interfaces for Admin, HR, and Employee users. The application was developed using a Flask backend, React frontend, and database-supported employee management modules. Testing covered authentication, APIs, frontend functions, database operations, and machine learning components, with 28 test cases successfully completed. The proposed system provides a unified approach for analyzing workforce risks and supporting data-informed HR decisions.

records.title: Stress reduction interventions for rural medical professionals – a narrative review
records.abstract: Introduction and Objective.Occupational stress and burnout affect over 70% of physicians globally, with rural practitioners facing additional stressors such as professional isolation, excessive workloads, and systemic under-resourcing.The aim of the review is to evaluate evidence on selected non-pharmacological stress-reduction interventions: meditation, mindfulness, yoga, progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), and breathing exercises, as practical strategies for rural medical professionals.Review Methods.A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed and Embase for English-and Polish-language publications (2010-2025).Grey literature from recognized health institutions was also consulted.Sources were selected based on credibility, relevance, and clarity.Brief description of the state of knowledge.The reviewed interventions reduce perceived stress, anxiety, and depression, and induce physiological effects, including lower heart rate and blood pressure, and lower cortisol.Mindfulness-based stress reduction showed moderate to large effects and improved quality of life.PMR proved effective regardless of session duration, suiting time-constrained clinicians.Breathing exercises, including cyclic sighing and diaphragmatic breathing, produced relief within five minutes.Yoga delivered both physiological and psychological benefits, though evidence for diagnosed anxiety disorders remains limited.Immersive technologies (VR/AR) may broaden access by eliminating travel barriers.Summary.Non-pharmacological interventions offer safe, accessible, evidence-supported strategies for managing occupational stress among rural physicians.Methodological heterogeneity, however, limits firm conclusions; standardized large-scale randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up are needed.

records.title: Status Quo of Artificial Intelligence- and Machine Learning-Supported Medical and Administrative Processes in Ambulatory Care Practice Management Systems: Systematic Review (Preprint)
records.abstract: BACKGROUND Electronic health records (EHRs) and practice management systems represent the digital foundation of outpatient care worldwide. Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-supported medical and administrative processes (AMP) into these platforms offers a profound opportunity to streamline clinical workflows and standardize patient care. However, existing research remains highly fragmented and focused on isolated tools. This creates a critical research gap, as there is currently no comprehensive mapping of how these diverse medical and administrative workflows collectively integrate and perform within the real-world clinical environment of ambulatory care. OBJECTIVE This study aims to address this research gap by comprehensively mapping the global status quo of natively EHR-integrated AMP in ambulatory care. Specifically, we explore the types of digital processes currently available and how physicians and medical assistants interact with these technologies in clinical environments. METHODS We conducted a systematic review of PubMed and Scopus databases (searching from inception to March 24, 2026) following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We targeted empirical studies evaluating outpatient clinical and administrative processes driven by AI, ML, or AI-enabled decision-support algorithms natively embedded within EHR or practice management systems. To ensure literature saturation, backward citation searching of included studies was conducted (yielding no additional eligible studies). Study selection, data extraction into a standardized matrix, and methodological quality assessment using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklists (tailored to RCTs, quasi-experimental, cohort, cross-sectional, and qualitative studies) were conducted by one reviewer and independently verified by a second reviewer. RESULTS A total of 39 empirical studies were included. Methodological quality assessed via JBI tools was moderate to high, with common limitations being a lack of participant and personnel blinding (system-inherent) and selection bias due to reliance on voluntary early adopters. Our synthesis identified 5 primary categories of natively EHR-integrated AMP: point-of-care clinical decision support systems (CDSS) (16/39, 41%), active background screening and triage (9/39, 23%), ambient intelligence for clinical documentation (8/39, 21%), administrative processes and patient communication (4/39, 10%), and remote patient monitoring (RPM) (2/39, 5%). While ambient AI demonstrated success in reducing documentation effort and burnout, point-of-care CDSS was heavily hindered by alert fatigue (with override rates up to 96%), and active background screening was constrained by algorithmic opacity (“black-box” characteristics) and clinician distrust. CONCLUSIONS Rather than achieving full automation, AMP technologies currently function as assistive tools within primary care. Real-world utilization requires a strict human-in-the-loop verification process, where medical professionals actively oversee both AI- and ML-driven outputs. Successful integration depends on addressing critical workflow barriers, particularly minimizing alert fatigue and enhancing algorithmic transparency to foster clinician trust. CLINICALTRIAL PROSPERO [CRD420261327094]

records.title: THE IMPACT OF FLEXIBLE WORK ARRANGEMENTS ON JOB PERFORMANCE: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF WORK LIFE BALANCE: AN EXPLORATORY STUDY OF A SAMPLE OF EMPLOYEES AT THE NORTH REFINERIES COMPANY
records.abstract: The study aimed to measure the effect of flexible work arrangements, its dimensions of spatial flexibility and temporal flexibility, on job performance, its dimensions of task performance and contextual performance, with the intermediary variable of work life balance, between the employees of the North Refineries Company in Iraq. The study used descriptive-analytical approach to attain the goal. The study subjects consisted of all employees of the company with a random representative sample of 238 male and female employees being selected. The main tool for collecting data from the participants was an electronic questionnaire. The data was analysed and the hypotheses tested through two statistical software packages: SPSS used to describe the study sample and to conduct a descriptive and diagnostic analysis of the study variables and SmartPLS 4 used to model a structural equation using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) approach. The study had several findings, the most significant of which was finding support for full and exclusive mediation of the relationship between spatial flexibility and job performance by the variable work life balance. This means that remote work does not automatically mean increased productivity efficiency unless there is a clear family/personal stability to the remote work first. Based on the findings, the study suggests to the North Refineries Company that they should adopt gender sensitive flexibility policies taking into consideration the social needs of female employees and progressively implement a flexible-hours policy rather than rigid attendance monitoring policies. It also suggests that remote-work policies should not be adopted for the sake of productivity alone but should be used as an organisational tool to minimise job burnout and make people healthier and happier in their work.

records.title: Temporal Quotas, Interrupted Task Resumption and Sleep Displacement in Generative AI Use
records.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems now serve as open-ended collaborators in coding, writing, study and planning. A conversational model can always produce another revision, so a working session has no natural end point. Emerging studies associate compulsive or problematic GenAI use with anxiety, burnout, cognitive overreliance and sleep disturbance, but the field remains conceptually fragmented and gives no grounds for treating "AI addiction" as a clinical diagnosis. Most of this work asks how much people use AI. This paper asks when they stop. It develops the Temporal-Quota Reinforcement Hypothesis (TQRH): short, predictable cycles of access replenishment, especially when the reset time is shown to the user, can act as temporal anchors that shape stopping decisions, anticipatory checking, return-to-use and bedtime in a susceptible subset of users. The hypothesis draws on research on problematic AI use, the I-PACE model, bedtime procrastination, the bidirectional relationship between technology and sleep, chronotype and the resumption of interrupted tasks. The paper makes five contributions: (i) operational definitions of quota events, reset-cue precision and the habitual sleep window; (ii) nine falsifiable hypotheses, with predictions that separate TQRH from five competing explanations, including the possibility that quota events merely mark heavy use; (iii) a two-phase protocol for Delhi-NCR that combines a four-week observational study (privacy-preserving metadata, ecological momentary assessment, sleep diaries and optional wearables) with a randomised interface experiment manipulating reset-time visibility and replenishment timing; (iv) an analysis plan with a smallest effect size of interest and equivalence-based falsification criteria; and (v) a design simulation showing that the number of quota events near bedtime, more than the number of participants, determines statistical power, so recruiting users who reach limits regularly is the most efficient design choice. The paper also separates consumer usage quotas from API rate limiting. TQRH does not claim that quotas cause insomnia. It proposes that the way an access architecture communicates future availability may change when people disengage, and it states the evidence that would show it does not.

records.title: The gap of psychological perspective in high-containment lab training — An exploratory systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: High-containment laboratories (HCLs) depend on sustained human performance to maintain biosafety and biosecurity, yet training primarily emphasizes technical competence and regulatory compliance while giving limited attention to human factors. We conducted an exploratory systematic review and meta -analysis to examine how laboratory personnel (LP) psychology can inform HCL training. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Ovid MEDLINE from inception to June 15, 2026. Two evidence streams were synthesized separately: HCL training studies and studies reporting psychological outcomes in LP. Risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Prevalence and odds ratios were pooled using random-effects meta -analysis (REML with Knapp–Hartung adjustment). Sixty-five studies met the inclusion criteria (38 HCL training; 27 psychology). Training literature was dominated by institution-specific programs, with limited international harmonization, inconsistent certification, infrequent incident-reporting frameworks, and minimal integration of psychological human factors. Leadership emerged as a recurring organizational factor influencing safety and well-being. Pooled prevalence estimates were 73% for stress (95% CI 51–88%), 45% for depression (27–65%), 44% for anxiety (22–68%), and 56% for burnout (31–78%). Compared with other healthcare workers, LP had higher odds of depression (OR 2.63, 95% CI 1.62–4.28) and anxiety (OR 2.57, 95% CI 1.73–3.83), whereas stress and burnout did not differ significantly. Current HCL training underrepresents psychological and organizational factors relevant to safe laboratory performance. Integrating evidence-based human factors, leadership, and mental health literacy into competency-based training and biosafety management may strengthen workforce resilience, operational reliability, and biosafety.

records.title: Editorial: Promoting mental health among healthcare professionals
records.abstract: Mental health among healthcare professionals has emerged as one of the most pressing occupational-health challenges of our era [1] . Long before the COVID-19 pandemic, sustained occupational strain, heavy workloads and the emotional toll of caring for vulnerable patients rendered healthcare workers at elevated risk of burnout, compassion fatigue, anxiety and depression. The pandemic dramatically exacerbated these stressors, and the psychological sequelae have persisted long afterwards [2] . This Research Topic compiles 33 articles, comprising original empirical investigations, cross-sectional and longitudinal surveys, group concept-mapping analyses, integrative reviews and systematic reviews. Collectively, these contributions advance scholarly understanding of mental health in the healthcare workforce by illuminating pathogenic mechanisms, protective psychological resources, context-specific vulnerabilities and implementable intervention pathways.Characterized by geographical and methodological diversity, the studies identify universal challenges while offering context-tailored solutions, generating a comprehensive evidence base for policymakers, healthcare administrators and clinicians striving to build a sustainable, mentally healthy workforce.Several contributions provide critical epidemiological evidence on the scope of mental health challenges facing healthcare workers. A landmark systematic review and meta-analysis [3] documented that the pooled prevalence of probable PTSD among healthcare workers was 15.5% prior to the pandemic, rising significantly to 24.8% during COVID-19, peaking in 2020 before returning to pre-pandemic levels in 2022.And school nurses in California during the pandemic [4] reported 40% burnout prevalence, with burnout severity significantly correlated with higher moral distress scores, driven largely by systemic barriers including inability to provide preventive care. Turkish nurses [5] experienced moderate COVID-19 phobia, with 46.8% languishing in the emotional subdimension, and gender, education, perceived health status, and intention to quit predicting 17% of phobia variance.In Sub-Saharan Africa [6] , burnout prevalence rates were reported as high as 54.5% in Tanzania and 68% in Malawi, underscoring how resource constraints and chronic staff shortages amplify vulnerability in low-resource settings. In conflict-afflicted areas, a study among Palestinian healthcare professionals [7] found anxiety prevalence of 51.5% and depression of 45.3%, revealing the compounding effects of war and political violence on mental health. Similarly, Ecuadorian medical residents [8] showed substantial burdens with 38.8% depression, 33.9% anxiety, and 12.1% hazardous drinking prevalence. Among Chinese residency trainees [9] , occupational burnout prevalence reached 70.48%, with 68.37% reporting at least one adverse practice experience-verbal abuse (51.51%), personal services demand (49.25%), and gender discrimination (47.14%) being the most common. Physical and emotional abuse exposures showed the strongest associations with burnout scores. Acupuncture practitioners in China's public hospitals [10] demonstrated moderate burnout levels, with emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment as primary dimensions, influenced by individual, organizational, occupational, and societal factors.Beyond these broad estimates, specific occupational contexts reveal distinctive patterns of risk. Intensive care unit professionals face compassion fatigue characterized by emotional exhaustion and reduced empathic capacity [11] . Psychiatric nursing involves high levels of emotional labor with dual pathways-surface acting (maladaptive) versus deep acting (adaptive)-with surface acting emerging as the primary bridge linking emotional labor to burnout [12] . The mediating role of emotion regulation, particularly cognitive reappraisal, was confirmed in the relationship between indecent work perception and burnout among psychiatric nurses, accounting for approximately 17% of the total effect [13] . Furthermore, occupational groups within emerging healthcare service models also exhibit distinctive risk profiles. A cross-sectional study focusing on nurses delivering "Internet+" home care services [14] revealed that this group reported low job burnout scores. But positive coping styles were negatively correlated with total burnout scores, whereas negative coping styles were positively correlated with total scores. These findings suggest that as healthcare service models undergo digital transformation, attitudes toward coping with burnout may become key to breaking the deadlock.A substantial cluster of studies investigated the protective factors that buffer healthcare workers against mental health deterioration. Social support and psychological resilience emerged as critical protective resources. One study [15] demonstrated that social support and psychological resilience significantly impact comprehensive wellbeing, with psychological resilience serving as a key mediator that enhances the positive effects of social support on overall wellbeing. In a related investigation [16] examining township healthcare workers in Lanzhou, sleep disorders were detected in 55.70% of participants, with social support playing a partial mediating role in the relationship between sleep quality and mental health (indirect effect proportion: 7.36%). These findings underscore the interconnectedness of sleep, social connectedness, and psychological resilience as interdependent pillars of mental health. A study of nurses in Chengdu [17] found that 35.7% reported anxiety, with psychological resilience partially mediating the relationship between social support and anxiety (accounting for 21% of the total effect); the pathway mediated by resilience was strongest for subjective support, with indirect effect constituting 41% of its total impact. Besides, the distinction between mentally active versus passive sedentary behaviors was explored among Chinese nurses [18] . Nurses engaging in mentally active sedentary behaviors-such as working, reading, hobbies, transportation, and chatting-for more than 4 hours/day had 47% lower odds of burnout compared to those with less than 1 hour/day. This inverse association remained after excluding transport-related sedentary behavior, while mentally passive sedentary behavior showed no significant association-a distinction offering practical, actionable guidance for workplace wellness initiatives.During crisis contexts, resilience and sense of agency were examined among Israeli healthcare professionals during mass casualty incidents and violent conflict [19] .Psychological capital and resilience were strongly associated with perceived agency, surpassing prior experience as predictors. Paramedics/EMTs reported higher agency than nurses/physicians, and spirituality also predicted agency. Empathy, a critical capacity in medical education, was found to have dual-pathway associations with mental health among medical students [20] . Empathy was positively associated with psychological distress, more rumination thinking, and better interpersonal competence.Interpersonal competence and rumination fully mediated the empathy-distress relationship-rumination linked to higher distress, while interpersonal competence was associated with reduced distress. The dynamic model of mental health proposed by one contribution [21] integrates stress, coping mechanisms, and resilience, incorporating individual, organizational, and socio-cultural factors, while emphasizing the importance of addressing moral dilemmas, high workloads, and systemic deficiencies.Several articles advanced the evidence base for interventions. A systematic review of biofeedback interventions for healthcare professionals [22] found consistent improvements in perceived stress, anxiety, depressive symptoms, emotional regulation, and resilience. Heart rate variability biofeedback and respiratory sinus arrhythmia training demonstrated the strongest effects, with physiological benefits including increased HRV, decreased sympathetic arousal, and improved autonomic balance. Despite methodological limitations including small sample sizes and heterogeneity, biofeedback was established as a feasible and potentially effective strategy for mitigating occupational stress.Digital mental health support needs were systematically analyzed using the Kano model among 1,571 Chinese nurses [23] . Of 26 identified needs, 8 were classified as must-be attributes, 8 as one-dimensional attributes, 7 as attractive attributes, and 3 as indifferent attributes. This nuanced framework provides a roadmap for designing digital mental health services that align with what nurses truly value and require. A cluster randomized controlled trial evaluated an integrated empowerment and narrative nursing program among 172 neonatal nurses [24] . The I-ENP group demonstrated significantly greater improvement in professional identity, with emotional exhaustion and depersonalization declining significantly and personal accomplishment increasing. These benefits were largely sustained at 9 months, and turnover intention was significantly lower in the I-ENP group A psychological program promoting posttraumatic growth was developed and validated among nursing trainees [25] , consisting of eight sessions addressing physical and emotional recognition, meaning-making, PTG reflection, happiness and value promotion, and hope inspiration. The treatment group showed increased PTG, resilience, mental wellbeing, and emotion processing post-intervention, maintained at follow-up, with a trend toward decreased burnout. Mental health literacy assessment was advanced through the validation of the Polish version of the Mental Health Literacy Scale among nursing students [26] . The 33-item MHLS-PL demonstrated good reliability, with independent predictors including age, education level, and interaction with persons diagnosed with mental disorders.Beyond individual-level interventions, several articles addressed organizational and systemic strategies. The integrative review on burnout management in Sub-Saharan Africa [6] synthesized evidence across Uganda, Mozambique, Botswana, and South Africa, identifying adaptive coping strategies-supportive supervision, workplace wellness activities, peer support, and culturally embedded coping practices-that enhanced motivation, job satisfaction, and emotional resilience. While self-distraction (traditionally labelled maladaptive) may be associated with lower burnout levels in the short term, prolonged use may mask underlying stressors and increase vulnerability to chronic burnout.The group concept mapping study with ICU professionals [11] generated five clusters of coping strategies: (1) meaning making through a person-oriented perspective; (2) supportive professional practice; (3) peer support and empathic teamwork; (4) work-life balance; and (5) personal responsibility.Peer support was rated highest in terms of use, while supportive professional practice was rated highest in importance but low in use-indicating an implementation gap that requires organizational attention.Work-family conflict among healthcare worker fathers during COVID-19 [27] was assessed across 2,844 fathers at four time points from 2020 to 2022. Fathers reported higher work-family conflict comparable to mothers, with risk factors including higher workload, exhaustion, moral concerns, and lower institutional trust. Exploratory longitudinal evidence pointed to a growing protective role of institutional trust against work-family conflict over time, underscoring that work-family conflict among HCW fathers is a structural issue requiring targeted workplace adaptations. Work-related wellbeing among hepatobiliary surgical nurses [28] was shaped by both occupational stress and internal psychological resources. Structural equation modeling demonstrated good fit, indicating that resilience and professional benefits had direct positive effects on wellbeing, occupational stress had a direct negative effect, and resilience and professional benefits partially mediated the impact of stress on work-related wellbeing.Family doctors' presenteeism [29] was negatively correlated with quality of work life and professional identity and positively correlated with job burnout. Hierarchical linear regression revealed significant impacts of work stress, professional behavior tendency, professional values, professional belonging sense, emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and professional efficacy on presenteeism. Among medical students in the post-pandemic era [30] , future work self-salience positively predicted occupational sense of mission, with professional identity partially mediating this relationship. Latent profile analysis identified three distinct profiles-high future work self-salience/high professional identity, moderate/moderate, and low/low-with the high/high profile exhibiting the highest occupational sense of mission.Young medical professionals' professional identity was examined within the New Quality Productive Forces framework [31] , with perceived social support significantly influencing professional identity (total effect b=0.625), comprising direct effect b=0.374 (59.80%) and indirect effect mediated by role cognition b=0.251 (40.20%).A conceptual analysis of new nurse workplace adaptation using Walker and Avant's method [32] identified three attributes: continuous dynamic adjustment, achievement of internal-external equilibrium, and integration into team collaboration. The analysis introduced the concept of "sacrificial adaptation"-a state where nurses compromise internal wellbeing for superficial integration-exposing a fundamental flaw in management strategies that prioritize behavioral compliance over authentic wellbeing.The provision of medication-free services within traditional mental health wards [33] was explored through qualitative focus groups, revealing an overall theme that medication-free services clash with a traditional medical system due to fundamental differences in philosophy, structure, power dynamics, and focus. Systemic changes were identified as necessary to create a more flexible, empowering, and relationship-focused milieu.Moral dilemmas during the COVID-19 pandemic [34] were examined from an organizational perspective, exploring how organizational structures, policies, and leadership influenced healthcare professionals' ethical decisions through processes of sensemaking and ethical suffering. A cross-sectional study of 8,071 physicians in Gansu Province's infectious disease sentinel institutions [35] found that coping style mediated the relationship between job satisfaction and burnout, while neurotic personality moderated these relationships, providing insights for targeted organizational interventions.Collectively, the 33 articles in this Research Topic paint a comprehensive picture of the mental health challenges facing healthcare professionals and the multifaceted strategies needed to address them. Several cross-cutting themes emerge. First, the burden is substantial and pervasive-from the 70.48% burnout prevalence among Chinese residency trainees [9] to the 51.5% anxiety among Palestinian healthcare workers [7] -yet it varies significantly across settings, roles, and contexts, demanding tailored rather than one-size-fits-all approaches. Second, protective factors operate at multiple levels: individual (resilience, coping strategies, mentally active behaviors), interpersonal (social support, peer relationships), and organizational (supportive supervision, work-life balance, institutional trust). Third, effective interventions span a spectrum from low-tech (peer support, narrative nursing, meaning-making) to high-tech (digital mental health, biofeedback), suggesting that diverse tools are needed to meet diverse needs. Fourth, the voices and lived experiences of healthcare professionals themselves must inform the design and implementation of support strategies-as demonstrated by the group concept mapping approach that enabled ICU professionals to define their own coping priorities [11] .As we look forward, several priorities warrant attention. Longitudinal research is needed to track how mental health trajectories evolve and how interventions exert their effects over time. Implementation science approaches can help bridge the gap between evidence and practice, particularly in resource-constrained settings-as highlighted by the implementation gap between high importance and low use of supportive professional practices [11] . Health-promoting behaviors [8] and mentally active sedentary behaviors [18] represent accessible, low-cost protective factors that can be integrated into daily routines. The concept of "sacrificial adaptation" [32] reminds us that genuine wellbeing cannot be achieved through superficial compliance alone.Ultimately, promoting mental health among healthcare professionals requires systemic change-not merely individual resilience training, but fundamental transformation of working conditions, staffing models, and organizational cultures that prioritize the wellbeing of those who care for us all. Special attention is called for comprehensive support systems, national policies, and cross-cultural research to improve healthcare workers' mental wellbeing [21] . Addressing both contextual and psychological factors is critical for reducing burnout and promoting sustainable professional development across healthcare settings worldwide.

records.title: Severity and Associated Factors of Alarm Fatigue Among Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alarm fatigue is a critical concern in intensive care units (ICUs), affecting nurse well-being and patient safety. It may reflect interacting conditions within the clinical work system, yet evidence on its severity and associated factors among ICU nurses remains fragmented. AIM: To synthesise evidence on alarm fatigue severity and associated factors among ICU nurses. STUDY DESIGN: Eleven databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Observational studies assessing alarm fatigue among ICU nurses using measurement tools with reported reliability were included. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed for alarm fatigue severity, stratified by instrument; associated factors and adverse outcomes were synthesised narratively using direction-of-association plots. RESULTS: ≈98%) and was not meaningfully explained by subgroup analyses or meta-regression. Directional evidence suggested that higher alarm fatigue was associated with a greater tendency towards medical errors and higher levels of burnout. Evidence on associated factors was mostly inconsistent or non-significant, with studies focusing mainly on person- and organisation-level factors. Poorer health, secondary traumatic stress, false alarms and lower trust in alarms tended to show adverse directional signals, whereas job satisfaction, resilience, alarm management support and a better nursing work environment showed potentially protective signals. CONCLUSIONS: Alarm fatigue among ICU nurses appeared to show a moderate tendency overall, although findings should be interpreted cautiously because of substantial heterogeneity. Evidence on associated factors remains scattered, with task-, technology- and environment-related factors comparatively underexplored. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: Alarm fatigue may be usefully considered from a clinical work-system perspective. Greater attention to task, technology and environmental factors may inform future practice improvement. REVIEW REGISTRATION: Prospero registration number: CRD42024565806.

records.title: Alarm fatigue severity and associated factors among intensive care unit nurses: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.abstract: Alarm fatigue is an important occupational and patient-safety concern in intensive care units (ICUs), where nurses are frequently exposed to false or non-actionable clinical alarms. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the severity of alarm fatigue among ICU nurses and synthesized associated factors and alarm-management interventions. The review followed PRISMA 2020 guidance and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261429354). Literature published from January 2001 to May 2026 was searched across major databases and grey-literature sources. ICU-specific studies reporting extractable alarm-fatigue scores were included in the quantitative synthesis. Scores from different instruments were transformed to a common 0–100%-of-maximum-possible (POMP) scale and pooled using a random-effects model. Associated factors were synthesized narratively because of methodological heterogeneity. Twenty-three studies were included, of which 11 contributed to the ICU-specific meta-analysis. The pooled normalized alarm-fatigue score was 51.66 (95% CI: 42.33–60.99), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 99.6%). Accordingly, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as an exploratory descriptive summary rather than a prevalence estimate or clinical threshold. Frequently reported factors associated with alarm fatigue included false and non-actionable alarms, high alarm burden, inadequate alarm-management knowledge and training, night shifts, overtime, workload, role overload, organizational limitations, and technology-related difficulties. Alarm fatigue was also associated with burnout, compassion fatigue, perceived stress, reduced nursing performance, and medical-error tendency. Randomized studies indicated that structured alarm-management education could reduce alarm fatigue and unnecessary alarm exposure. Alarm fatigue is a substantial and multifactorial concern among ICU nurses. However, confidence in most reported associations remains limited by predominantly cross-sectional, self-reported, and heterogeneous evidence. Further prospective studies incorporating objective alarm data and validated patient-safety outcomes are needed. This systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in PROSPERO under registration number CRD420261429354. Not applicable.

records.title: Application of Large Language Models in the Whole‑Process Management of Lung Cancer: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Lung cancer is the malignant tumor with the highest incidence and mortality worldwide, and has become a major public‑health issue that seriously endangers human health. According to the GLOBOCAN 2024 report jointly released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) and the American Cancer Society, there were approximately 2.6 million new lung‑cancer cases and 1.9 million deaths, accounting for 12.8 % of the total global cancer incidence and 19.1 % of total global cancer mortality respectively, ranking first among all cancer types. It is projected that cancer incidence will rise by 67 % by 2050 compared with 2024. Lung‑cancer management has long been one of the most challenging topics in oncology. First, such complexity stems from the intrinsic biological heterogeneity of lung cancer. Non‑small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC) differ fundamentally in molecular mechanisms, clinical behaviours and treatment responses. NSCLC is further subdivided into multiple subtypes including adenocarcinoma, squamous‑cell carcinoma and large‑cell carcinoma. Each subtype features distinct mutational profiles of driver genes such as TP53, KRAS, EGFR and ALK. Such molecular diversity directly necessitates individualised treatment strategies. Second, lung‑cancer management requires multidisciplinary collaboration. With the rapid advances in targeted therapy and immunotherapy, therapeutic options have expanded greatly, yet the complexity of clinical decision‑making has increased exponentially. Clinicians must strike precise trade‑offs among rapidly updated clinical guidelines, emerging clinical‑trial evidence and the unique clinical profiles of individual patients[3]. Furthermore, the growing complexity of clinical documentation exacerbates clinician burnout. Patients with lung cancer often suffer substantial psychological distress and have high information‑related needs. Against this backdrop, the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers new technical opportunities to address the complex challenges in lung‑cancer management. Boasting ultra‑large‑scale parameters, extensive pre‑training corpora and powerful natural‑language‑processing capabilities, LLMs demonstrate great potential in clinical settings. Although existing reviews have preliminarily summarised the applications of LLMs in lung‑cancer diagnosis and treatment, they cannot fully capture the breadth of application scenarios, heterogeneity of evaluation approaches and unaddressed research gaps within this fast‑evolving field. A scoping review is a methodological tool designed to map the full body of evidence in a given domain and identify the distribution of research themes and key concepts. This paper conducts a scoping review on the applications of LLMs in lung‑cancer management. It focuses on analysing LLM types, clinical scenarios, task formats, evaluation metrics and perspectives, and discusses limitations of current studies and directions for future research. It aims to provide systematic references for healthcare workers and researchers, and lay a foundation for subsequent technology translation, clinical practice and policy‑making.

records.title: A Comparative Study of Mental Health and Employee Performance Across Service Sector Industries
records.abstract: Employee mental wellness is now a key performance indicator, especially in fast-paced service industries where stress levels are high. Titled "A Comparative Study of Mental Health and Employee Performance Across Service Sector Industries," this research delves into the connection between employees' mental health and their performance in five prominent service sectors: IT, healthcare, education, banking, and hospitality. Stratified random sampling of 500 employees from various industries was used to deliver structured surveys that included standardized mental health evaluations (e.g., GHQ-12) and employee performance measures. The research was conducted using a quantitative, comparative methodology. The study is based on the idea that a person's mental health has a direct impact on their productivity and the performance of their organization as a whole. The complex relationship between mental health disparities and performance outcomes is the focus of this research, which seeks to shed light on the role of industrial dynamics. In order to find similarities and differences across different industries, statistical procedures such as ANOVA, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis were used. Findings showed substantial sector-specific differences; for example, hospital and banking workers reported much greater levels of stress and burnout, which were found to be inversely connected to performance indicators. Despite worries about emotional exhaustion and work-life balance, employees in the education and information technology industries indicated modest levels of mental health. Because of these distinctions, it is essential to implement proactive, industry-specific mental health efforts. Organizations can boost employee happiness and output by dealing with the sources of psychological distress. Insights gained from these results can help human resources experts and company executives develop targeted mental health interventions that boost productivity in the workplace. In order to maintain a productive workforce over the long term, the study stresses the strategic value of incorporating mental wellness practices into company culture. The scope could be broadened in future studies by comparing cultures, doing longitudinal analyses, and investigating the mediating role of organizational support systems. To further enhance our understanding of effective intervention design, qualitative investigations on employee views of workplace mental health resources could be conducted.

records.title: Occupational Stress Management and Pastoral Performance among Catholic Priests in the Diocese of Kitale, Kenya
records.abstract: Abstract: Occupational stress is increasingly recognised as a threat to clergy wellbeing and ministerial effectiveness, yet the pathways through which stress-management resources translate into pastoral performance remain under-examined in African dioceses. This study investigated the influence of four stress-management resources (psycho-spiritual support, self-care practices, work–life balance, and institutional support) on the pastoral performance of priests in the Catholic Diocese of Kitale, Kenya. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design combined an ex-post facto quantitative survey of 61 priests, drawn through stratified random sampling from a target population of 104, with in-depth interviews among eight purposively selected key informants. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and simple and multiple linear regression, interpreted against Erikson’s psychosocial development theory, Maslach’s burnout theory, role theory, and the transactional theory of stress and coping. The four predictors jointly explained 48.5% of the variance in pastoral performance, R² = .485, F(4, 55) = 12.977, p < .001. Institutional support was the strongest individual predictor (β = .381, p = .001), followed by work–life balance (β = .344, p = .003), self-care practices (β = .289, p = .009), and psycho-spiritual support (β = .267, p = .011). Priests relied more heavily on personally initiated resources, notably prayer and informal peer support, than on formalised diocesan structures. Sustaining pastoral effectiveness in resource-constrained dioceses appears to require deliberate institutional investment, including structured leave, accessible counselling, and workload management, rather than reliance on individual clergy resilience alone. Keywords: occupational stress management; pastoral performance; institutional support; work–life balance; Catholic priests; Kenya.
