records.title: Att främja gymnasiestuderandes välbefinnande : En undersökning av ”Studera starkt” – en multikomponent intervention inom positiv psykologi
records.abstract: This doctoral dissertation explores the potential of a multicomponent positive psychology intervention (MPPI) to enhance the well-being and thereby the academic ability of general upper-secondary school students in Finland. In response to increasing concerns over adolescents’ declining life satisfaction and growing mental health problems, this research contributes to the development of effective, school-based strategies that support psychological well-being as a fundamental part of education. Student well-being is a vital component of educational success and directly influences academic motivation and performance. If schools do not foster well-being, they risk limiting students’ ability to engage fully in learning. The dissertation consists of two quantitative studies conducted between 2020 and 2022 across ten schools, which utilized a partly randomized controlled design and statistical analysis of survey data. The intervention—a course combining principles from positive psychology and cognitive therapy, tailored to fit the educational setting, was collaboratively developed by the research team and the participating teachers. It comprised 17 lessons, each lasting 75 minutes, and was delivered by the school staff. Study I (N = 343) examined the immediate and long-term effects of the intervention on student well-being, and its immediate effects on their ill-being. The results indicated small, immediate improvements in the students’ experiences of positive practices at school and in their happiness and positive emotions. However, they did not indicate any immediate effects on all the aspects of well-being, nor any on ill-being, including negative emotions, depression, or study-related burnout. Due to the absence of a control group in the follow-up measurement, the small long-term improvements in general well-being should be interpreted with caution. Notably, the students reported benefiting both academically and personally from the course, with 92.6% indicating they would recommend it to others. Study II (N = 342) examined whether student characteristics (gender, baseline ill-being) or levels of engagement in the intervention (homework completion, mindfulness practice, intervention attendance, and mode of delivery—in-person or remote) influenced the outcomes. No significant moderation effects were observed from baseline to post-intervention, but a significant interaction between time, gender, and meditation frequency emerged at follow up, which affected overall well-being. Moreover, frequent meditation was linked to increased well-being among boys but decreased or minimal changes among girls. Furthermore, completion of homework was positively associated with perceived intervention benefits for well-being and with intervention usefulness in both the studies and in personal life, whereas frequent meditation showed a surprising negative correlation with perceived intervention usefulness in the studies. These findings suggest that personal motivation plays a key role in maximizing the impact of interventions, and that a flexible approach to implementation can be effective. This dissertation underscores the substantial potential of schools that foster student well-being. The findings show that school-based MPPIs can enhance well-being and thereby improve study capacity, while also potentially preventing student ill-being. Future programs should aim for rigorous designs and clear objectives to avoid inefficiency and to ensure meaningful outcomes. The dissertation also advocates for ongoing collaboration between researchers and schools to implement and refine cost-effective, evidence-based practices to promote youth mental health. In Finland—where the national core curriculum emphasizes student well-being—schools are uniquely positioned to adopt holistic solutions that go beyond academic achievement and support students’ overall development. In line with the curriculum’s focus on equality, schools also have both the responsibility and the opportunity to address disparities in well-being that may arise from differences in students’ backgrounds.

records.title: Artificial intelligence-driven work systems and employee burnout: a systematic review of mechanisms, moderators, and a dynamic meta-system framework.
records.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into workplace systems is transforming job design and employee experiences. While AI promises efficiency gains, it also creates a paradox by simultaneously reducing workload and increasing psychological strain, leading to divergent effects on burnout. This study systematically reviews evidence on the relationship between AI exposure and employee burnout and develops the AI as Meta-System (AIMS) framework. Following PRISMA 2020, four bibliographic databases and Google Scholar were searched from inception to 31 March 2026. Forty-three peer-reviewed primary empirical studies were included: 20 measured burnout or an established burnout dimension, and 23 examined mechanisms, moderators, proxy outcomes, measurement, or implementation conditions. Methodological quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool at the criterion level. Findings varied according to the functional role of AI and the study design. Assistive AI was generally associated with lower burnout or exhaustion in randomized and pre-post healthcare studies, whereas monitoring and algorithmic-control exposures were associated with greater burnout or related psychosocial strain in observational studies. Perceptual AI exposure produced direct, indirect, and null associations through pathways involving job stress, job insecurity, work-family interference, perceived organizational support, and organizational commitment. Three randomized studies provided the strongest evidence for assistive interventions. Evidence for nonlinear effects was limited to supporting proxy outcomes and did not directly establish an inverted U-shaped AI-burnout relationship. Artificial intelligence is not inherently harmful or beneficial; its associations with burnout depend on its functional role, implementation, and employee appraisal. The AIMS framework integrates these pathways and identifies propositions requiring longitudinal and experimental testing.

records.title: Benefits of Training Volunteers in Mental Health Promotion Within Organisations Employing People with Disabilities: Preliminary Results.
records.abstract: Background: Psychosocial factors present in various work environments can pose a risk to workers' health, but those with some form of disability may be more vulnerable and more severely affected by these issues. Objective: The goal of this study is to assess whether training employees to act as health promoters, as well as providing them with follow-up support, can help to improve health outcomes among other workers and serve as a link between them and healthcare professionals. Method: Initially, 148 employees were recruited from five centres belonging to the same company, in which the majority of staff had some form of disability or were at risk of social exclusion. Three centres were randomly assigned to the intervention group and two centres formed the control group (waiting list). Measurements were taken at three time points (baseline, at six months and at twelve months). Initially, 82 people participated from the intervention group, and at the two subsequent time points, 69 and 55 respectively. From the control group, 49 employees participated in the baseline assessment and, at the two subsequent time points, 37 and 32 respectively. The following instruments were used: (1) a demographic and employment data form; (2) the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12); (3) the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI General Questionnaire); and (4) five items from the Columbia Scale for the Assessment of Suicidal Severity. Results: The intervention group showed improvements in all variables over time and also in comparison with the control group. These improvements were statistically significant in terms of general health and in the dimensions of cynicism and professional efficacy. Conclusions: The establishment of mental health promotion teams within organisations can help to improve key aspects of employees' psychological wellbeing, which encourages further research in this field to investigate the effectiveness of structured and sustainable interventions.

records.title: A scoping literature review of factors associated with burnout among student pharmacists in the United States.
records.abstract: Burnout is an increasing challenge among student pharmacists. Individual studies have examined burnout among student pharmacists; however, faculty and college administrators lack a consolidated understanding of the educational, personal, and contextual factors associated with burnout. This scoping literature review explored factors associated with burnout among student pharmacists in the United States. For this scoping literature review, MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and PsycINFO were searched for English-language studies published between January 2000 and February 2026. Records were deduplicated in EndNote and Covidence. Eligible studies reported factors associated with burnout or related outcomes, including emotional exhaustion, anxiety, depression, and poor well-being. Quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies were included. Two independent reviewers screened studies, assessed full texts, and extracted data, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Reporting followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria from 2893 screened records. Most were published since 2020, used observational survey designs, and included students from one or more United States colleges of pharmacy. Validated burnout measures, primarily the Maslach Burnout Inventory and Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, were commonly used. Burnout was associated with intrinsic program factors (year in program, workload, competitive culture, campus assignment), extrinsic factors (co-curricular activities, employment, career planning), and individual factors (sex, marital status, sleep, nutrition, resilience, lack of time). One randomized trial found a mindfulness application reduced burnout after six weeks, although longer-term effects were mixed. Burnout requires systemic curricular reform, integrated wellness initiatives, and longitudinal, multi-institutional research to improve student well-being and reduce burnout.

records.title: A Personalized Recovery Intervention to Support Sleep Health in Emergency Healthcare Professionals.
records.abstract: Optimizing sleep health in healthcare professionals is a challenge, as misalignment between endogenous circadian rhythms and exogenous work schedules undermines recovery, well-being, and performance. This study evaluated a tailored recovery intervention based on cognitive-behavioural approaches for insomnia designed to support recovery to rotating night shifts. In a randomized controlled trial (REST), 72 emergency healthcare professionals were randomized to intervention or control. The intervention combined personalized sleep-wake feedback with stress management techniques. Sleep-wake rhythms were monitored via actigraphy for 3 weeks before and 1 week after the intervention. Outcomes included objective sleep duration, self-reported sleepiness, insomnia severity, and subjective sleep quality, measured using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Insomnia Severity Index, and Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire. Fifty-nine participants (28 intervention, 31 control) were included in the primary analyses. Even on free nights, average nocturnal sleep duration was 6 h and 21 min, below recommended levels for adults. Compared with controls, intervention participants increased nocturnal time in bed by 37 min, 95% CI [13, 62], p = 0.003, and total sleep time by 23 min, 95% CI [4, 42], p = 0.019. Perceived sleep quality also improved for the intervention group t(55) = -7.91, p < 0.001, d = 2.06, 95% CI [1.42, 2.70], and insomnia symptoms decreased (β = -2.23, 95% CI [-4.26, -0.21], p = 0.031). These findings suggest that structured occupational recovery programs can enhance sleep health and facilitate recovery across rotating night work schedules. Integrating such interventions into training may reduce burnout, improve safety, and support workforce sustainability.

records.title: Education and training interventions for healthcare workers to prevent sexual harassment.
records.abstract: Sexual harassment is common among healthcare workers and is associated with poor mental health, job dissatisfaction, and workforce attrition. Education and training may help prevent sexual harassment, but their effectiveness in healthcare settings has not been systematically evaluated. To assess the effectiveness of education and training interventions on knowledge and skills for managing sexual harassment, and to assess their impact on the incidence of sexual harassment towards healthcare workers in healthcare settings. We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, AMED, CINAHL, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP, together with reference checking and contact with study authors, to identify eligible studies. The latest search date was March 2025. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving healthcare workers comparing education or training interventions with control (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention) or different types of education or training to prevent sexual harassment in healthcare settings. Our critical outcomes were knowledge and skills in managing sexual harassment and the incidence of all types of sexual harassment perpetrated by patients, visitors, coworkers, and management. Important outcomes were anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, and perception of the organisational climate related to harassment. We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess risk of bias. We synthesised results for each outcome using random-effects model meta-analysis. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome. We included two studies from Taiwan with a total of 170 nurses. Most participants were young women with little work experience. The intervention group received education to prevent sexual harassment, and the comparison group received a different type of education to prevent sexual harassment. We found no studies that had a comparison group without any active educational or training components. Education and training interventions to prevent sexual harassment compared to control (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention) in healthcare workers No studies addressed this comparison. Education and training interventions to prevent sexual harassment compared to other education and training interventions for healthcare workers We found two studies reporting on education and training interventions to prevent sexual harassment compared to other education and training interventions in healthcare workers. Educational interventions to prevent sexual harassment probably increase sexual harassment prevention knowledge slightly ('sexual harassment prevention', mean difference (MD) 4.74, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.21 to 8.28; P = 0.71; I2 = 0%; 2 RCTs, 168 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and may increase management skills slightly ('coping behaviour', MD 6.36, 95% CI -6.84 to 19.56; P = 0.43; I2 = 0%; 2 RCTs, 168 participants; low-certainty evidence) and ('prevention strategy', MD 11.70, 95% CI 2.56 to 20.85; P = 0.22; I2 = 33%; 2 RCTs, 168 participants; low-certainty evidence). No study evaluated the incidence of sexual harassment, anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, or perception of the organisational climate related to harassment. Adverse effects were not measured or reported in the included studies. The certainty of the evidence was moderate to low. We judged the overall risk of bias as low, and we identified no inconsistency or publication bias. However, imprecision was more of a concern given the low number of participants and relatively broad CIs around the effect estimates. Healthcare workers may benefit from education and training compared to another type of education and training. The benefits were modest and were measured as increased knowledge ('sexual harassment prevention') and management skills ('coping behaviour' and 'prevention strategy'). The certainty of the evidence is moderate to low, and future studies could make the findings more robust. There is a need for future studies investigating other types of outcomes such as anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, and perception of the organisational climate related to harassment. It would also be valuable to assess a wider range of healthcare workers, as we only found studies in nurses. No studies addressed the effects of education and training compared to control groups (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention). The decision to offer sexual harassment education and training to healthcare workers is supported by the existing evidence. However, other contextual factors may also be considered, as well as healthcare workers' preferences to participate in educational activities. This Cochrane review had no dedicated funding. Registration: Cochrane Collaboration, 19th of December 2023. Education and training interventions for health care workers to prevent sexual harassment. Identification number: EMID:9ba735d2b5367171. Authors: Therese K Dalsbø, Rakel Aasheim Greve, Ingrid L Jørgensen, Marita S Fønhus. Published on the 6th of February 2025 available via Cochrane Library at https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD016096.

records.title: Efficacy and Safety of Saffron and Ashwagandha for Stress-Related Mental Health Outcomes: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
records.abstract: Saffron (Crocus sativus L.) and ashwagandha (Withania somnifera Dunal) are medicinal plants with emerging clinical evidence supporting their use for stress-related mental health conditions. This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review, prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261385134), synthesizes randomized controlled trial evidence for both plants across eight mental health outcomes, with the literature search updated to 31 August 2026. From 494 initial records, 452 remained after duplicate removal; 34 studies met eligibility criteria (19 saffron, 14 ashwagandha, 1 comprehensive review), comprising 31 randomized controlled trials. Saffron demonstrated efficacy for depression (10 randomized controlled trials [RCTs]), anxiety (9 RCTs), and sleep (8 RCTs) at 15-30 mg/day standardized extract. Ashwagandha showed efficacy for anxiety (10 RCTs), stress (8 RCTs), and sleep (3 RCTs) at 30-600 mg/day with a withanolide-standardized extract, with a pooled cortisol reduction of -3.27 µg/dL. Risk of bias was low in 10 of 31 trials and raised some concerns in most of the remainder, and GRADE certainty was moderate at best. Both plants exhibited favorable safety profiles, although ashwagandha-associated hepatotoxicity warrants liver enzyme monitoring during prolonged use. Critically, no RCTs exist for burnout or posttraumatic stress disorder in either plant, despite mechanistic evidence of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis normalization, reduced neuroinflammation, and monoaminergic and gamma-aminobutyric acid-ergic modulation; this evidence is predominantly preclinical and requires clinical confirmation. This systematic review identifies these conditions as priority targets for well-designed clinical trials. The bioactive constituents-crocin and safranal in saffron, and withanolides in ashwagandha-share overlapping mechanistic pathways highly relevant to these underserved, high-burden disorders.

records.title: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study Comparing ChatGPT to Live Coaching Deliberate Practice to Teach Difficult Conversations.
records.abstract: Poor performance during difficult conversations is associated with decreased patient satisfaction and increased clinician burnout. Communication skills can be taught using simulated patients (SPs), but this approach is resource intensive. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a potential adjunct for communication training. However, its role within anesthesiology education and structured communication curricula remains unclear. We conducted a randomized controlled pilot study involving anesthesiology trainees, including anesthesiology residents and student registered nurse anesthetists, at a tertiary pediatric hospital. All participants completed a didactic session on the SPIKES framework, followed by deliberate practice using either OpenAI's ChatGPT or an SP with live instructor feedback. Participants completed pretraining and posttraining assessments using a validated 16-item communication skills checklist with an SP. Self-reported knowledge, confidence, and ability to apply communication skills were assessed using Likert-scale surveys. Twenty-five trainees were enrolled (ChatGPT n = 13; SP n = 12). Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in checklist scores following training. Self-reported knowledge, confidence, and application of communication skills improved in both groups. A curriculum combining didactic instruction with deliberate practice using either ChatGPT or SPs was associated with improved simulated communication performance among anesthesiology trainees. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of incorporating AI-based tools into communication training.

records.title: Effects of transcendental meditation on mental health and work productivity among university staff in Australia: A randomised controlled trial.
records.abstract: Chronic psychological stress is a major public health problem with adverse effects on mental health, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and work functioning. Transcendental Meditation (TM) is a standardised meditation that may reduce stress and enhance wellbeing, yet long-term evidence in workplace settings is limited. This study evaluated the effect of TM on perceived stress and related outcomes among Australian university staff. This two-arm, open-label randomised controlled trial enrolled staff of an Australian university into TM (5-day training plus regular practice, n = 65) or control (usual wellbeing resources, n = 64) groups. Symptoms of perceived stress (primary outcome), anxiety and depression symptoms, workplace burnout, poor sleep, well-being, HRQoL, and productivity impairment were assessed at baseline, 3, and 6 months. Analyses were conducted using baseline-adjusted linear mixed models under the intention-to-treat principle. TM significantly reduced perceived stress over 6 months compared with control (adjusted mean difference - 2.25 [95% CI: -3.33, -1.17], p < .001) with a moderate effect size (Hedge g = -0.52). Significant improvements were also observed in symptoms of anxiety, depression, burnout, sleep quality (mean differences -0.25 to -2.89), well-being, and HRQoL (1.08 to 1.64). Exploratory analysis showed that twice-daily practice was significantly associated with improvements in perceived stress, well-being, HRQoL, symptoms of depression and burnout (p < .05). No adverse effects were reported. TM produced significant improvements in stress, mental health, sleep, and HRQoL over six months and warrants consideration as a safe, effective workplace mental health strategy, but active-comparator trials with longer follow-up are needed.

records.title: Compassion-Focused Therapy for Mothers of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: Impact on Parental Burnout, Self-Criticism, and Psychological Distress.
records.abstract: Mothers of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently experience a substantial caregiving burden that heightens their vulnerability to parental burnout, harsh self-criticism, and severe psychological distress. This study evaluated the efficacy of compassion-focused therapy (CFT) in reducing parental burnout, self-criticism, and psychological distress among mothers of children with ASD. A pretest-posttest experimental design with a waitlist control group and a 3-month follow-up was employed. The target population consisted of mothers of children with ASD attending rehabilitation centers, psychology clinics, and autism associations in Ahvaz, Iran, in 2025. Using purposive sampling, 64 eligible mothers were recruited and randomly assigned to the experimental or control group (n = 32 per group). The experimental group received eight weekly 70-min CFT sessions, while the control group received no intervention. Data were collected using the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale-Third Edition (GARS-3), Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA), Forms of Self-Criticising/Attacking and Self-Reassuring Scale (FSCRS), and 21-item Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21). Repeated measures ANOVA revealed significant main effects of time and group, along with significant time-by-group interactions across all variables. At posttest, CFT significantly reduced parental burnout, self-criticism, and psychological distress in the experimental group compared with the control group (p<.01). These gains were maintained at the 3-month follow-up, demonstrating the intervention's enduring efficacy. The findings indicate that CFT is an effective intervention for alleviating these psychological burdens. Integrating CFT into family support programs is strongly recommended to enhance the long-term psychological well-being of mothers raising children with ASD.

records.title: Paws for relief: A pilot randomized controlled study of animal assisted therapy's effect on pediatric ICU healthcare workers' stress and anxiety.
records.abstract: Animal assisted therapy (AAT) decreases stress, anxiety, and improves overall well-being in healthcare workers (HCW). However, little is known about its effects on pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) HCW, who experience higher risks for burnout, compassion fatigue, and acute stress compared to other specialties. This pilot randomized controlled and feasibility study examined the impact of AAT on PICU HCW's perceived stress and anxiety during a clinical shift. Thirty-two PICU HCWs were randomized to a 15-min AAT session with a facility dog and child life specialist or a 15-min break. Participants completed measures of stress (visual analog scale for stress) and anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory) at baseline (T1), immediately after the intervention (T2), and 6 h later (T3). Quantitative data were analyzed using t-tests, and feasibility feedback was reviewed. The AAT group demonstrated significantly greater reductions in stress and state anxiety at T2 compared to controls. No sustained differences were observed at 6 h (T3), with a rebound in state anxiety noted in the AAT group. Despite logistical barriers, participants described AAT as beneficial, restorative, and feasible with staffing support. AAT produced immediate reductions in stress and anxiety among PICU HCWs but did not demonstrate sustained effects over 6 h. AAT is a promising wellness intervention, though future research should test more frequent AAT and incorporation with other support strategies. AAT may provide a feasible strategy for immediate stress relief among PICU HCWs and could be incorporated into broader staff wellness initiatives.

records.title: Research Trends in Publications on Yoga and Meditation Interventions for Nurses' Mental Well-Being and Work Productivity: A Bibliometric Analysis.
records.abstract: ObjectiveTo map publication trends and the thematic, geographical, and collaborative structure of research on yoga, meditation, and related contemplative practices among nurses.MethodsA bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Scopus database. The search combined terms relating to mental well-being, stress, burnout, quality of life, productivity, yoga, meditation, mindfulness, mind-body interventions, and nursing personnel, with publication years restricted to 2015-2024 and English-language records. Data were analyzed using Microsoft Excel and VOSviewer to examine annual publication trends, leading journals and authors, geographical distribution, co-occurrence patterns, and collaboration networks. Screening and data extraction were conducted by the first author using predefined eligibility criteria, with multiple rounds of verification during data cleaning. The absence of independent dual-reviewer screening is acknowledged as a limitation.ResultsA total of 382 articles met the inclusion criteria and were published in 63 peer-reviewed journals from 46 countries. About 15% of the studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs); the rest were quasi-experimental, pre-experimental, reviews, and conceptual/theoretical papers. In 14 of these articles, the names of countries were not mentioned, although some authors were contacted by mail for this information; however, they declined to provide it. The primary result is a threefold increase in publications over the last 10 years across all study designs, with the major ones being controlled studies, RCTs, cross-sectional studies, and meta-analyses. Most publications originated from the United States (n = 143), followed by China (n = 23) and the United Kingdom (n = 18). The findings also show that the USA has 16 times as many research publications as India. The top three authors were Kemper, K.J., Chesak, S.S., and Sawyer, A.T., and the top three journals were Holistic Nursing Practice (n = 19), Journal of Holistic Nursing (n = 19), followed by International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (n = 13).ConclusionResearch on nurses' well-being and contemplative practices has grown substantially, with mindfulness and psychological well-being emerging as dominant themes. Geographical, collaborative, and thematic gaps indicate scope for broader and more integrated research within holistic nursing.

records.title: Optimizing generative artificial intelligence for clinical summarization: a blinded comparison study of automated versus human care planning synopses.
records.abstract: Data, information, and knowledge in health care has expanded exponentially over the past 50 years, leading to significant challenges with information overload and complex, fragmented care plans. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to facilitate summarization and integration of knowledge to enable efficient care planning and reduce cognitive load of clinicians. To determine the value of AI generated summarization through optimization of short synopsis creation at care transitions. Blinded, randomized comparison study comparing human- vs AI-generated synopses using the data-information-knowledge-wisdom framework. De-identified records of 64 patients with multiple chronic conditions from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III database. Accuracy, succinctness, synthesis, and usefulness of synopses using a standardized scale with scores > 80% indicating success. Artificial intelligence and clinicians summarized 64 patients with 12% overlap. In blinded trials, AI synopses were rated as useful 75% of the time vs 76% for human synopses. AI had lower succinctness ratings for the data synopsis task (55%-67%). For accuracy and synthesis, AI had near equal or better scores in other domains (AI: 72%-79%, humans: 68%-84%), with best scores from AI in wisdom. Interrater agreement was variable. Artificial intelligence-created synopses that were nearly equivalent to human-created ones; they were slightly longer and did not always synthesize individual data elements compared to humans. We showed that expert-guided optimization of an open-source large language model can lead to synopses that match those produced by humans, reducing cognitive load.

records.title: A Systematic Review of Psychosocial Interventions for Enhancing Resilience in Medical Sciences Students.
records.abstract: Undergraduate medical sciences students experience substantial psychological distress due to demanding academic workloads and early clinical exposure, increasing their vulnerability to anxiety, depression, and burnout. This systematic review evaluates randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining psychosocial interventions-including mindfulness-based programs, cognitive-behavioral strategies, acceptance-based therapies, and structured stress-management training-designed to enhance resilience among undergraduate medical sciences students. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, ISI Web of Science, ProQuest, Google Scholar, and Semantic Scholar identified studies published between January 2000 and April 2025. 11 RCTs met inclusion criteria. Data extraction included participant characteristics, intervention type and duration, delivery format, and outcome measures. Methodological quality was assessed using the PEDro scale, and risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Across the included trials, psychosocial interventions demonstrated consistent positive effects on resilience, perceived stress, coping flexibility, and psychological well-being. Mindfulness-based programs-ranging from brief sessions to full 8-week MBSR courses-generally reduced distress, though shorter or peer-led formats produced mixed results. Cognitive-behavioral and stress-management interventions improved coping skills, emotional regulation, and self-efficacy. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy enhanced psychological flexibility, and structured resilience curricula such as the Penn Resilience Program yielded significant gains in resilience scores. Variability in intervention design, duration, and measurement tools limited comparability across studies. Overall, psychosocial interventions appear effective in enhancing resilience among undergraduate medical sciences students. Integrating structured, theory-based approaches into medical education may strengthen students' psychological health and academic functioning. Future research should prioritize standardized protocols, culturally sensitive adaptations, and long-term follow-up.

records.title: Beyond Ergonomics Training: Added Effects of a Supervised, Equipment-Free Workplace Exercise Program on Musculoskeletal Symptoms, Sleep, and Burnout in Artisanal Pastry Workers: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.abstract: To determine whether adding a supervised exercise program to workplace ergonomics education adds benefit for musculoskeletal, sleep, and burnout outcomes in börek (Turkish pastry) workers. In this exploratory randomized controlled trial (NCT07447180), 60 male börek masters from 47 Istanbul shops were randomized to ergonomics education alone or education plus a 12-week supervised, equipment-free exercise program. The primary outcome was the number of symptomatic body regions (Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire). Symptomatic regions decreased with added exercise (4.73 to 3.17) but not with education alone (baseline-adjusted difference, -1.41; 95% CI, -1.94 to -0.87). All secondary outcomes (QuickDASH, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Maslach Burnout Inventory) favored added exercise. Supervised exercise added to ergonomics education produced a moderate incremental reduction in musculoskeletal symptom burden; all outcomes were self-reported by unblinded participants, so objective confirmation is required.

records.title: Mapping Workplace Mental Health Practices: A Scoping Review and Preliminary Conceptual Synthesis for the Brazilian Context.
records.abstract: To map evidence on workplace mental health practices for promotion, prevention, screening, and management of mental health and psychosocial risks, with attention to their potential relevance to the Brazilian occupational context. A scoping review followed JBI guidance and was reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Cochrane Library. Studies, protocols, and institutional documents published between 2020 and 2025 addressing workplace mental health practices in occupational settings were included. Sixty-eight records were included. Relatively stronger evidence for short-term psychological outcomes came from moderate-robustness randomized studies of ACT and resilience training. Mindfulness was more frequently studied but showed heterogeneous and mostly short-term effects. Evidence for exercise, CBT-based self-care, coaching, and leadership interventions was preliminary or mixed. Effect sizes, sustained benefits, and organizational outcomes were inconsistently reported. The mapped literature was heterogeneous and concentrated on individual-level approaches, with limited assessment of organizational outcomes. Five recurring domains were organized as a hypothesis-generating conceptual synthesis to support future consensus development, contextual adaptation, feasibility assessment, and implementation research in Brazil. This synthesis is not a validated model or recommendation for routine practice.

records.title: Impact of ontological coaching on well-being, job outcomes, and retention intentions in nurses: A multi-centre randomised controlled trial.
records.abstract: Nurses are at risk for poor psychological outcomes due to work-related burnout and stress. Since supportive interventions such as coaching have been found to improve nurses' overall well-being, an ontological coaching intervention was developed to improve nurses' well-being. To investigate the effects of an Ontological Coaching among Nurses intervention on nurses' psychological well-being (primary outcome), occupational stressors, social support, goal-setting proficiency, intention to leave nursing, and job satisfaction (secondary outcomes). Multi-centre, two-group parallel-armed randomised controlled trial with baseline, intermediate, and post-intervention measurements. Data were collected from public tertiary hospitals and primary care public outpatient clinics (polyclinics) under the National University Health System Cluster in the Central and Western region of Singapore between December 2023 and October 2024. Four hundred nurses, aged 21 and above, working in the NUHS, were recruited and randomly assigned to either an intervention group (n = 200) or a control group (n = 200). The intervention group received the Ontological Coaching among Nurses intervention, comprising one group coaching session followed by four individual coaching sessions, in addition to the standard support available to nurses. The control group received only the standard support provided by their respective hospitals or organisations. At baseline, all participants completed a sociodemographic questionnaire. Outcome data were collected at three time points: baseline (during recruitment), intermediate intervention (after two individual coaching sessions), and post-intervention (after four individual coaching sessions). Between-group differences were analysed using general linear models. After adjusting for baseline, recruitment site and intervention, participants in the intervention group also reported higher psychological well-being (mean difference (MD) = 8.70, 95% CI: 5.38 to 12.02, p < 0.001), goal-setting proficiency (MD = 1.88, 95% CI: 0.28 to 3.49, p = 0.02), job satisfaction (MD = 11.22, 95% CI: 2.59 to 19.85, p = 0.01), and lower intention to leave nursing (MD = 1.05, 95% CI: 1.74 to 0.37, p = 0.003) at post-intervention. At the intermediate timepoint, nurses in the intervention group reported a statistically significantly higher psychological well-being (MD = 2.93, CI 95%: 0.17 to 5.68, p = 0.04) and job satisfaction (MD = 8.24, 95% CI: 0.82 to 15.66, p = 0.03), and lower intention to leave nursing (MD = 0.76, 95% CI: 1.39 to 0.13, p = 0.02). The Ontological Coaching among Nurses is a feasible and promising intervention to enhance nurses' psychological well-being, goal-setting skills, job satisfaction, and retention intentions. It could be integrated into workplace well-being programmes, with refinement to address occupational stressors and social support. Future research should adopt cluster randomisation, use shorter validated tools to reduce survey fatigue, include objective retention measures, and assess long-term outcomes. https://clinicaltrials.gov/ (NCT06878157).
